_comment: Routes that exist ONLY in the desktop build. This is NOT a Go golden, and
it is the one file in this directory that is not.
read_routes.json and write_routes.json were generated by a chi.Walk over
the router server.New built, and #391 froze them when the Go tree was
deleted. Neither can record a route Go never had without ceasing to be
what it is -- a record of Go's surface. Leaving the desktop-only routes in
no file at all was the alternative, and it was rejected: those files exist
so the route surface cannot drift silently, and a whole family recorded
nowhere would weaken exactly that property.
So this file is the third table, with the same row shape and one stronger
guarantee. The two Go files are asserted in ONE direction -- the Rust test
iterates their rows, so a route that is claimed and never recorded passes.
Here the module under test exposes its routes as a single const (see
native::security::ROUTES) and the assertion is set equality, so a route
cannot be added, removed or renamed without this file moving.
'status' is 'native' or 'dropped', as in read_routes.json. Nothing is
'deferred': there is no second implementation left to defer to.
Nothing regenerates this file. It is authored alongside the code, and the
test is what keeps the two honest.

routes.reason: fires a configured task on demand -- the one thing the product could not do, since the only way to make a task run was to change its schedule type to run_immediately and so destroy the schedule being tested. Answers 202 with the job_history id the run will write rather than blocking for the run itself, which reaches 240 minutes; 409 when a run of that task is already in flight; and a PAUSED task is deliberately runnable, which is most of the point. It advances nothing the schedule owns -- not run_count, not next_run_at, not the stop_after_count budget
the public key, its kid and where both files live; write-scoped, because it names the private key's path
replaces the install's keypair, which refuses every token ever issued including the caller's own
the issued tokens, revoked ones included; write-scoped, because it enumerates every credential on the machine
mints a scoped token and returns the only copy of it that will ever exist
revokes one token by jti; an UPDATE rather than a DELETE, because removing the row would un-revoke it
the public key in JWKS form, UNAUTHENTICATED by design -- it is what a credential is verified against, so requiring one would be a bootstrap problem with no answer
the enable toggle, the port and start-with-app; read-scoped, because it names no secret
stores the three and reloads the listener; a port below 1024 is refused before anything is written
the configured providers through the PUBLIC projection -- api_key is a boolean computed in SQL, never a value
creates a provider with its API key; answers through the public projection, so the key it just stored is not echoed
updates a provider; an OMITTED api_key preserves the stored one, which is what stops the PUT /api/integrations/{id} credential-wipe being reproduced here
deletes a provider, or 409s naming the aliases still routed to it -- routing refers to providers by name inside a JSON column, so no foreign key can catch this
the model aliases and their ordered targets and fallbacks
creates an alias; a target naming no configured provider is refused rather than stored to fail at request time
updates an alias; checks the row exists first, because store_alias upserts and would otherwise create silently on a PUT
deletes an alias by row id, not by alias string -- nothing stops two rows sharing an alias
running / stopped / bind_failed / start_failed plus the port and the reason; a STORED value, so a port collision is distinguishable from a gateway that is simply off

is 127.0.0.1:N bindable, and if not what is the next port that is -- the one thing the settings form cannot answer for itself, because a webview cannot bind a socket. Advisory by nature (a port free at probe time can be taken before the bind), so Status::BindFailed stays the authority; what it buys is that the routine collision is reported BEFORE the save rather than after it. The running listener's own port reads as available, or the user could never re-save their own configuration

the model ids that provider's own upstream reports, so an alias target is picked rather than typed; the only route here answered by the ASYNC registry, because it makes an outbound HTTPS call -- and the answer is ids alone, never the key and never the upstream body

asks a provider's own free list-models endpoint whether a credential is one it accepts, so a typo is caught at the form rather than as a 401 inside whichever tool was pointed at the gateway; an OMITTED api_key checks the stored one, so an existing provider is re-testable without a secret the user can no longer retrieve. Answered by the ASYNC registry, like the catalog route it shares its dialects with -- and with 200 whatever the verdict, because the outcome of the check is what was asked for
windowed aggregates over gateway_usage_log, bucketed in the request's timezone; unpriced requests are surfaced as a count, never folded into the cost total as zero
